definition: Data-oriented parsing (DOP, also data-oriented processing) is a probabilistic model in computational linguistics.
details: DOP was conceived by Remko Scha in 1990 with the aim of developing a performance-oriented grammar framework. Unlike other probabilistic models, DOP takes into account all subtrees contained in a treebank rather than being restricted to, for example, 2-level subtrees (like PCFGs), thus allowing for more context-sensitive information. Several variants of DOP have been developed. The initial version developed by Rens Bod in 1992 was based on tree-substitution grammar, while more recently, DOP has been combined with lexical-functional grammar (LFG). The resulting DOP-LFG finds an application in machine translation. Other work on learning and parameter estimation for DOP has also found its way into machine translation.

explainer.lead: Data-oriented parsing is a way to build a probabilistic grammar directly from a collection of parsed sentences. It can reuse tree fragments of many sizes, allowing larger patterns and more contextual information to influence an analysis than in a conventional PCFG.

tiers.eli5: Imagine learning language from a box of sentence diagrams. Instead of keeping only tiny pieces, you keep pieces of every size, from small phrases to much larger patterns. Data-oriented parsing uses those pieces to judge which new sentence diagrams are most likely.
tiers.practitioner: DOP starts with a treebank and considers all subtrees it contains, rather than only the two-level subtrees used by PCFGs. Implementations vary: Rens Bod's initial 1992 version used tree-substitution grammar, while DOP-LFG and related learning and parameter-estimation work have been applied to machine translation.
tiers.paperLevel: DOP is a probabilistic grammar model whose fragment set comprises all subtrees contained in a treebank, rather than being restricted to local PCFG-style productions. Remko Scha conceived DOP in 1990 as a performance-oriented grammar framework; Rens Bod's initial 1992 version was based on tree-substitution grammar. Later variants include DOP-LFG, which combines DOP with lexical-functional grammar.

explainer.example: Suppose a treebank contains parse trees for "the cat sleeps" and "the dog sleeps." When analyzing "the cat sleeps," DOP can draw on small pieces such as the noun-phrase structure as well as larger subtrees spanning more of the sentence, with the probabilistic model taking those available fragments into account.

usedIn.name: Machine translation
usedIn.detail: DOP-LFG and other work on DOP learning and parameter estimation have found applications in translation.

usedIn.name: Performance-oriented grammar modeling
usedIn.detail: DOP uses analyses collected in a treebank as the basis for a probabilistic grammar framework.

explainer.intuition: A treebank contains reusable grammatical patterns at many scales. DOP keeps that range of patterns available, so a parse can reflect both small local structures and larger, more context-sensitive ones.
howItWorks: Begin with a treebank of parsed sentences.
Consider all subtrees contained in its parse trees.
Use these fragments in a probabilistic grammar model.
Let larger fragments contribute context that local PCFG rules cannot capture.
Choose a variant such as tree-substitution DOP or DOP-LFG for the target setting.
explainer.whyItMatters: DOP shows how a grammar can retain rich structural evidence from example analyses instead of reducing every tree to small local rules. Its variants also connect this idea to machine translation and lexical-functional grammar.
misconceptions: DOP is not limited to the two-level subtrees associated with PCFGs.
DOP is not one fixed implementation; several variants have been developed.
Data-oriented parsing and data-oriented processing refer to the same approach here.

diagram.caption: DOP turns the full range of subtrees in a treebank into the basis of a probabilistic grammar, with several variant frameworks.
